title: Jeremiah 5:20–31
context: Jeremiah 5:20–31 continues the LORD’s message, addressed to the house of Jacob and Judah. He calls them foolish people who have eyes but do not see and ears but do not hear, and asks whether they will not fear the one who set the sand as a boundary for the sea. Yet the people have rebellious hearts and do not fear the LORD who gives rain and harvest; their sins have withheld good from them. Wicked men among the people trap others like fowlers, grow rich and fat through deceit, and refuse to defend the fatherless and the needy. The LORD repeats his question whether he should not punish such a nation, and he ends by describing a horrible thing in the land: prophets prophesy falsely, priests rule by their own authority, and the people love to have it so. Both traditions read this unit as joining idolatry, social injustice, and corrupt leadership in one indictment.

verses.text: “Declare this in the house of Jacob, and publish it in Judah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to declare this in the house of Jacob and publish it in Judah. Arminian readers see God continuing to speak to his people, giving them clear warning before judgment comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the command as part of Jeremiah’s prophetic commission. Both traditions note that the names Jacob and Judah recall the people’s covenant history and identity, which makes their unfaithfulness more serious.

verses.text: ‘Hear this now, foolish people without understanding, who have eyes, and don’t see, who have ears, and don’t hear:
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls the people foolish, having eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear. Arminians see spiritual dullness that comes from persistent refusal to listen, which leaves people unable to perceive the truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see spiritual blindness as both the people’s fault and part of God’s judgment. Both traditions note the similar language in Isaiah 6:9–10 and in Jesus’ words in Mark 8:18, and they treat the theme as shared ground.

verses.text: Don’t you fear me?’ says the LORD; ‘Won’t you tremble at my presence, who have placed the sand for the bound of the sea by a perpetual decree, that it can’t pass it? Though its waves toss themselves, yet they can’t prevail. Though they roar, they still can’t pass over it.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks whether they will not fear and tremble before him, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea by a perpetual decree. Arminian readers see God’s power in creation as a reason to fear him, which the people have ignored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign decree in ordering creation. Both traditions note the contrast the passage draws: the sea obeys its boundary though its waves roar, but God’s people do not obey him.

verses.text: “But this people has a revolting and a rebellious heart. They have revolted and gone.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the people have a revolting and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone away. Arminians see the human heart as the source of rebellion, which leads people away from God even when he has shown his power and care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as part of Jeremiah’s teaching on the corrupt heart (compare 17:9). Both traditions affirm that the problem lies within, and that the people are responsible for their rebellion.

verses.text: They don’t say in their heart, ‘Let’s now fear the LORD our God, who gives rain, both the former and the latter, in its season, who preserves to us the appointed weeks of the harvest.’
verses.arminianNotes: The people do not say in their hearts that they will fear the LORD, who gives rain in its season and keeps the weeks of harvest. Arminian readers see ingratitude for God’s daily gifts, which should have led the people to worship him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence in the seasons as testimony to his goodness. Both traditions note that the people may have credited the rain to other gods, and they read the verse as showing that the LORD alone provides.

verses.text: “Your iniquities have turned away these things, and your sins have withheld good from you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says their iniquities have turned these good things away and their sins have withheld good from them. Arminians see a link between covenant faithfulness and blessing, which fits the warnings of Deuteronomy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God withholding blessing as a form of discipline. Both traditions note that this verse speaks of the covenant nation’s corporate life, and they avoid turning it into a rule that every hardship is caused by a specific sin.

verses.text: For wicked men are found among my people. They watch, as fowlers lie in wait. They set a trap. They catch men.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says wicked men among his people lie in wait like fowlers and set traps to catch people. Arminian readers see the exploitation of the weak by the powerful, which the prophets condemn as a serious covenant violation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing schemes of injustice. Both traditions hold that oppression of neighbors is a breach of God’s law, and they read the verse as part of the indictment against Judah’s society.

verses.text: As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit. Therefore they have become great, and grew rich.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says their houses are full of deceit, like a cage full of birds, and so they have become great and rich. Arminians see wealth gained through deceit, which God sees and will judge though the wicked seem to prosper.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as exposing unjust gain. Both traditions note the continuing image of the fowler from verse 26, and they read the prosperity of the wicked as temporary under God’s justice.

verses.text: They have grown fat. They shine; yes, they excel in deeds of wickedness. They don’t plead the cause, the cause of the fatherless, that they may prosper; and they don’t defend the rights of the needy.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they have grown fat and sleek, excel in wickedness, and do not defend the fatherless or the rights of the needy. Arminian readers see the failure to care for the vulnerable, which the law required of God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see justice for the fatherless and needy as central to covenant faithfulness (compare Deuteronomy 10:18). Both traditions hold this as shared ground and read the verse as one of the main reasons for the coming judgment.

verses.text: “Shouldn’t I punish for these things?” says the LORD. “Shouldn’t my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks again whether he should not punish such a nation and be avenged. Arminians see the repeated question from verse 9, now applied to social injustice as well as idolatry, showing that both offend God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the repetition as emphasizing the certainty of God’s justice. Both traditions read the refrain as inviting the hearers to recognize that judgment is deserved.

verses.text: “An astonishing and horrible thing has happened in the land.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says an astonishing and horrible thing has happened in the land. Arminian readers see God’s shock at the depth of corruption among his people, which prepares for the description of their leaders in the next verse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the language as expressing the seriousness of the people’s sin. Both traditions read the verse as introducing the final indictment of the chapter, which focuses on prophets, priests, and people together.

verses.text: The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority; and my people love to have it so. What will you do in the end of it?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the prophets prophesy falsely, the priests rule by their own authority, and his people love it so, and he asks what they will do in the end. Arminians see leaders and people sharing guilt, since the people chose leaders who told them what they wanted to hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as exposing a people content with falsehood. Both traditions hold the people responsible for loving false prophecy, and they read the closing question as a warning that judgment will come.
